blocks.text: The second is that of Jonathan and of the Jerusalem Targum: the one of them has here מינקת חויא, and the other פלית חויא, or פיילת חויא. So it should be read, not חיוא, in the Lexicon of Baal-Aruch. The lexicographers understand neither. For it is [II, 488] beside the point that they take פליית here for a locust, as in פליא ביארי in chapter 9 of the Talmudic tractate On the Sabbath. For פליא ביארי is one thing, פליית חויא another. Namely, the very thing that the Arabs call فالية الافاعي [fāliyat al-afāʿī] phaliath alaphai, that is, the searcher of serpents, or of vipers (they taught us above ^{b)} that this name is given to a painted kind of beetle which usually lives with scorpions and serpents in the lair of the land crocodile), that very thing, I say, is the Chaldee פליית חויא. For to them חויא is serpent, and פליית paljath, or phaljath, is plainly derived from the Arabic فالية [fāliya] phaliath, which we render searcher, because فلي [falā] phala means to search. Thus فلي الراس [falā al-raʾs] he searched the head, to look for lice in it; [col. 1065] فلي الشعر [falā al-shiʿr] he searched the poem, that is, he explored and examined it in order to penetrate the poet's mind. And this kind of beetle is rightly said to search the serpents, since it lives continually with them in the same lair, and so constantly accompanies the serpents, whether coming or going, in such a way that by its arrival or its departure it signals whether they are near or away. Hence the proverb current among the Arabs: اتكلم فالية الافاعي [a-takallama fāliyat al-afāʿī] Have you spoken to the phaliath alaphai, the searcher of serpents? It is used لاول شر ينتظر بعده شر منه [li-awwal sharr yuntaẓar baʿdahu sharr minhu] of a first evil after which another is expected to arise from it. But since the verb فلي [falā] phala means not only to search but also to nourish and to rear, Jonathan has, instead of פליית חויא, מינקת חויא, i.e. the nurse of the serpent. Further, why the two Chaldee translators wished this kind of beetle to be designated by the word אנקה anaka, I see no reason except the very order of the words. Namely, as the word צב tsab signifies the land crocodile, as we have proved at length ^{c)}, so the following אנקה anaka seemed to signify פליית חויא, that is, the searcher of the serpent, which is the constant companion of the land crocodile and usually lives in the same lair with it. But this reason, such as it is, carries little weight with me, as does the version itself, which seems to rest on it. Something I had almost omitted: for some of the Arabs these little creatures are not beetles but بنات وردان [banāt wardān] benath vvardan, which is what Abenbitar calls the σίλφας [silphas] of Dioscorides, or blattae [cockroaches].
